record.context_brief: Separating true and finite prosoluble kernels
record.original_question: Determine whether there exists a discrete group Γ that is both residually finite and residually soluble, so that the canonical maps Γ -> PF(Γ) and Γ -> PS(Γ) are injective, but for which the canonical map Γ -> PFS(Γ) to the prosoluble completion built from finite soluble quotients is not injective.

evidence.quote: (6.G) Does there exist a discrete group Γ which on the one hand is residually finite and residually soluble, namely for which both homomorphisms Γ −→ PF(Γ), Γ −→ PS(Γ) are injective, and which on the other hand is such that the homomorphism Γ −→ PFS(Γ) is NOT injective?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a discrete (abstract) group. Define the following three completions of Γ:

(i) The profinite completion PF(Γ) is the inverse limit of the finite quotients Γ/N, where N runs over the normal subgroups of finite index in Γ.

(ii) The prosoluble completion PS(Γ) is the inverse limit of the soluble quotients Γ/N, where N runs over the normal subgroups of Γ for which Γ/N is soluble.

(iii) The profinite soluble (finite-soluble) completion PFS(Γ) is the inverse limit of the finite soluble quotients Γ/N, where N runs over the normal subgroups of finite index in Γ such that Γ/N is soluble.

There are canonical homomorphisms Γ → PF(Γ), Γ → PS(Γ), and Γ → PFS(Γ). The map Γ → PF(Γ) is injective iff Γ is residually finite; the map Γ → PS(Γ) is injective iff Γ is residually soluble.

Question: Does there exist a discrete group Γ that is simultaneously residually finite and residually soluble (so both Γ → PF(Γ) and Γ → PS(Γ) are injective), yet such that the canonical homomorphism Γ → PFS(Γ) fails to be injective?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in work on the true prosoluble completion of groups. Web searches surface the same paper containing the question but no follow-up resolution; some sources note that examples of groups residually finite and residually soluble where Γ → PFS(Γ) is not injective are known, but a definitive published resolution of this specific formulation could not be confirmed.
